reception.text: The Surface Creek Champion of Cedaredge reported that the Gunnison News-Champion and several Gunnison citizens were objecting "in very strong language" to the reserve, claiming it had been made through the influence of sheepmen.
The same Delta County paper answered from experience with its own reserve that it was "working an immense amount of good" in "preserving the forests and holding water."

The Gunnison News-Champion kept up the attack, pointing to evidence from the Oregon land-fraud trials that sheep interests had sought to enlarge a forest reserve at the cattlemen's expense, and suggesting that all sorts of influences were at work in making reserves.

reception.text: The press record found for 1905 is regional, not national: Oregon's Morning Oregonian on the Idaho reserves and western Colorado papers on the Gunnison reserve.
In April 1905 the Oregonian's Washington bureau reported more than four million acres in Idaho withdrawn "pending the creation of new forest reservations."

political_impact.text: The Transfer Act put the reserves under the Secretary of Agriculture, leaving surveying, entry and patenting with the General Land Office.
The agricultural appropriation act funded the bureau under the new heading "FOREST SERVICE" from July 1, 1905, and gave reserve employees power to make arrests for violations of reserve rules.

Senator Weldon B. Heyburn of Idaho objected that farm and mineral land had been swept into the Idaho withdrawals. In July the Oregonian reported he had written Pinchot half apologizing for his opposition, though he did not accept the administration's policies.

By late September Heyburn was arguing that a separate, still-pending Shoshone County withdrawal was settled farmland; a General Land Office special agent reported the claims were timberland and most claimants lived in Wallace, Heyburn's home town.

West-central Colorado, home of the Gunnison, Uncompahgre, Cochetopah and Holy Cross reserves, was by one regional history's account a "hotbed of anti-forest reserve agitation," led in Washington by Senator Henry M. Teller.
political_impact.source: Bureau of Land Management, The Valley of Opportunity, ch. 9

political_impact.text: The new Forest Service announced grazing fees, first charged in 1906, which stockmen resented more than any boundary.
By the General Land Office's year-end figures the reserves grew from 59 reserves of 62,763,494 acres in 1904 to 83 reserves of 85,627,472 acres in 1905, an increase of nearly 23 million acres.
political_impact.source: Gates, History of Public Land Law Development (1968), p. 580
